title: How does EF Core detect changes and what does SaveChanges do?
description: Change tracking internals, DetectChanges, when to disable tracking, and batched SQL under the hood.

data.text: **Question:** How does EF Core detect changes and what does SaveChanges do?

EF Core keeps a **snapshot** (or proxy-based notification) of each tracked entity. During `DetectChanges` it compares current property values against the snapshot and marks entities Added/Modified/Deleted. `SaveChanges` then translates those states into `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` statements inside **one transaction** and commits. Nothing reaches the database until you call it — and nothing tracks in read-only scenarios unless you ask it to.

**The tracking lifecycle:**
- Entities enter the **change tracker** when queried (default) or when you `Add`/`Attach`
- On `SaveChanges` (and at other sync points), EF runs **DetectChanges**: current values vs the loaded snapshot → state per entity
- States: `Added` (insert), `Modified` (update), `Deleted` (delete), `Unchanged` (ignored), `Detached`
- After a successful save, states reset to `Unchanged` and new identity/key values are written back
- The DbContext is **not** thread-safe and is meant to be short-lived — one per unit of work/request

**When tracking costs you:**
- Every tracked entity pays snapshot + bookkeeping memory and DetectChanges time
- Read-only queries (dashboards, exports, lists) should opt out: `AsNoTracking()`, or globally via `QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking`
- Projections into DTOs (`Select(u => new UserDto {...})`) are never tracked anyway — often the cheapest read path
- `ChangeTracker.Clear()` in long-running hosts (background workers, Blazor circuits) to prevent an ever-growing context

**Bypassing the pipeline on purpose:**
- `ExecuteUpdate` / `ExecuteDelete` (EF Core 7+) run set-based SQL directly — no tracking, no round-trips, single statement for bulk edits
- Bulk operations over thousands of tracked `SaveChanges` updates are an anti-pattern: batch size is limited, transaction time grows, memory balloons

data.title: Tracking vs no-tracking vs set-based updates

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing nothing happens on property assignment — only on SaveChanges
- Understanding where tracking overhead comes from and when to turn it off
- Awareness that DbContext is a scoped, unit-of-work object, not a static gateway
- Knowing the set-based escape hatch (ExecuteUpdate/Delete) for bulk work

items: Calling SaveChanges after every property set instead of once per unit of work
Using one long-lived DbContext across requests or threads — thread-safety and stale snapshots
Tracking entities in heavy read-only queries out of habit
Looping 10,000 SaveChanges calls (or a 10k-entity single save) instead of ExecuteUpdate or SqlBulkCopy
Assuming Attach() validates the entity — it just marks it Unchanged/Modified by convention
Expecting relationships to fix themselves without loading or fixing up the related entities
How does EF Core know which properties actually changed when it writes the UPDATE?
What is the difference between SaveChanges and SaveChangesAsync — when does async actually help?
How would you update 100,000 rows with EF Core without loading them?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: DetectChanges diffs snapshots into Added/Modified/Deleted states
SaveChanges batches those states into one transaction
AsNoTracking/projections for read-only work; Clear() in long-lived hosts
data.takeaway: EF Core's pipeline is a unit-of-work: track only what you'll write, save once per transaction, and bypass tracking entirely for reads and bulk work.
